title: Zorvath Kael
context: Zorvath Kael is a celebrated glass-shaper of the Ehlmoor Reach, renowned for his spiral kilns and the revival of tidal annealing. In his youth he was apprenticed to the master artisan Vronila Teshk, under whom he trained for eleven years before opening his own atelier at Admerion. Kael's registered guild callsign is Brintaq, a mark now stamped on every vessel he completes. He works only during the twilight tides, and his lattice goblets are prized across the Reach for their faint humming resonance. Late in life Kael took seven apprentices of his own and codified the Twelve Temperings, a manual still studied by the guild.

title: Vronila Teshk
context: Vronila Teshk was a master artisan of the early Reach period, born in the town of Qelmoor Vast, where her family kept a small kiln beside the salt canals. She pioneered the technique of lattice-glass and founded the Teshk Atelier, which trained a generation of shapers. Teshk was known for her insistence on silence in the workshop and for the pale blue tint she coaxed from marsh ash. Her surviving notebooks describe forty-one distinct annealing schedules. She never married, devoted herself entirely to the craft, and in her final decade served as arbiter of the guild's quality court.

title: Mirelle Danthos
context: Mirelle Danthos is an astronomer of the Cindral Plateau, best remembered for charting the drift of the Ochre Comet. As a young scholar she studied under the reclusive stargazer Oqquin Vale, accompanying him on nine winter expeditions to the high mirrors. Danthos's observatory ledger is filed under the catalog mark Threx-9. She proposed that the plateau's twin moons share a single slow orbit, a claim debated for decades. Beyond her charts she built the great brass astrolabe of Sennreth and tutored the plateau's first class of women navigators. Her measurements of the ochre drift remain the standard reference.

title: Oqquin Vale
context: Oqquin Vale was a stargazer of severe habits, born in the city of Yllandor on the far salt coast. He kept no students for most of his life, preferring the solitude of the high mirrors, and compiled the first complete atlas of the winter sky. Vale was famous for refusing lamplight, insisting the eye must learn true darkness. He catalogued over three thousand faint stars and named the Ochre Comet after the color of the dawn it heralded. In his last years he grew nearly blind and dictated his final atlas to a single scribe.

title: Bastien Ulvgrenn
context: Bastien Ulvgrenn is a cartographer of the Drenn Marches, known for the first accurate survey of the shifting fen roads. He was trained by the veteran mapmaker Serapha Nooq, who taught him to measure distance by the cadence of a walking mule. Ulvgrenn signs his charts with the cipher mark Vodrel. His maps introduced the dotted tide-line convention now used throughout the Marches, and he is credited with locating the lost causeway to Emberhold. Though he traveled little in his final years, his apprentices carried his methods to the coastal provinces, where fen-style surveying is still practiced.

title: Serapha Nooq
context: Serapha Nooq was a veteran mapmaker born in the village of Dremmit Hollow, a cluster of turf houses at the edge of the great fen. She spent forty years surveying terrain others thought unmappable and devised the rolling chain still used to measure marsh distance. Nooq was known for her fierce temper and her habit of redrawing any map she deemed careless. She produced the celebrated Atlas of Nine Waters and trained a handful of chosen students in the walking-cadence method. She died on the road, mid-survey, with her final chart unfinished.

title: Kaelira Vonn
context: Kaelira Vonn is a bell-founder of the Ossler tradition, celebrated for the deep-toned carillon of Hadmere. She was a disciple of the elder founder Tremaug Ossler, from whom she learned the secret alloy the guild calls river-bronze. Vonn's foundry stamps each bell with the sigil Marrenq. She is credited with casting the largest bell ever hung in the eastern valleys and with reviving the double-strike tuning method. In addition to her founding work, Vonn wrote a treatise on resonance that circulates among instrument makers far beyond her home valley.

title: Tremaug Ossler
context: Tremaug Ossler was an elder bell-founder born in the town of Wexforge, where his family had worked the forges for six generations. He perfected the river-bronze alloy that gave the region's bells their unusual warmth and cast instruments for shrines across three valleys. Ossler was a patient, secretive man who tested every bell alone at midnight. He refused to sell his alloy formula and passed it only to a few trusted disciples. His masterwork, the Vigil Bell, is said to be audible from the far ridge on still nights.

title: Pellandor Krise
context: Pellandor Krise is a composer of the Amber Court, known for his tide-cycle symphonies performed at the equinox festivals. He was mentored by the court musician Vashti QLoren, who introduced him to the seven-string resonant lute. Krise's scores are archived under the seal Ondrimu. His most famous work, the Nine Tides Suite, is said to imitate the rhythm of the harbor bells. Beyond composing, Krise reformed the court's system of musical notation and trained a small circle of players devoted to his layered style. He is regarded as the last great composer of the Amber Court's late period.

title: Vashti QLoren
context: Vashti QLoren was a court musician born in the port of Ammavault, a busy harbor town famed for its bell towers. She mastered the seven-string resonant lute and served three successive courts before settling at the Amber Court as senior musician. QLoren was celebrated for improvising for hours without repetition and for her insistence that music must answer the tide. She composed little but taught widely, shaping a generation of players. In her later years she curated the court's vast archive of songs and mentored several promising young composers.

title: Orsen Dukalt
context: Orsen Dukalt is an apothecary of the Vermil guild, known for the fever tinctures that carry his mark. In his youth he was apprenticed under the formidable alchemist Iyzabel Cthonn, who schooled him in the distillation of marsh essences. Dukalt seals his vials with the emblem Perrik. He is credited with isolating the pale salt that steadies the heartbeat and with founding the first free dispensary in the lower town. Though cautious by nature, Dukalt kept meticulous records, and his casebooks are still consulted by the guild's younger members.

title: Iyzabel Cthonn
context: Iyzabel Cthonn was a formidable alchemist born in the city of Grishlow, raised above her family's dye works amid vats of strange color. She became the foremost authority on marsh essences and ran a crowded laboratory that trained many of the region's apothecaries. Cthonn was known for her exacting standards and her refusal to publish anything she could not reproduce ten times. She discovered the binding agent still called Cthonn's mordant and served for years as the guild's chief examiner. She worked until the very end, mixing tinctures by candlelight.

title: Tavigan Reld
context: Tavigan Reld is a harbor pilot of the Sarnnok coast, famed for guiding grain ships through the treacherous Neck shoals. He was the protégé of the master pilot Nimue Astraq, who taught him to read current by the color of the foam. Reld's pilot license bears the number Sarnnok-4. He charted a new deep channel that shortened the northern run by two days and served as harbormaster during the great storm season. Known for his calm under pressure, Reld trained many younger pilots and rarely lost a vessel to the shoals.

title: Nimue Astraq
context: Nimue Astraq was a master harbor pilot born in the town of Ospremoor, a windswept settlement of fishers and rope-makers. She spent her life on the Neck shoals and became the most trusted pilot on the coast, credited with saving dozens of ships from the shifting sandbars. Astraq was famous for navigating by foam-color alone and for her uncanny memory of the seabed. She trained a small number of protégés in her methods and served as senior pilot until she was well past seventy. Her logbooks remain a standard text for coastal pilots.

title: Halvard Sween
context: Halvard Sween is a master falconer of the Kelspar highlands, renowned for training the rare silver harriers used in the autumn hunts. He was a pupil of the old falconer Corabel Yrix, who taught him the whistled commands passed down in her line. Sween's hunting register is marked with the token Elgrist. He developed a gentler method of manning wild-caught birds and served as falconer to the highland warden for many years. Sween is also remembered for writing a short, much-copied primer on the care of moulting hawks, still used by highland falconers.

title: Corabel Yrix
context: Corabel Yrix was an old master falconer born in the village of Tunvael, high among the wind-scoured crags where the silver harriers nest. She spent seventy years with the birds and was regarded as the last keeper of the whistled command-line. Yrix was severe and solitary, trusting few people and fewer students. She refined the autumn hunt into a precise ritual and kept a famous mews of forty harriers. She took only a handful of pupils in her lifetime and guarded her whistled signals jealously, teaching them only to those she deemed worthy.

title: Delphine Marogh
context: Delphine Marogh is a tapestry weaver of the Ombrist looms, known for her shadow-weft portraits that seem to shift with the light. As a young woman she studied under the exacting master weaver Yssora Belnokh, spending six years at her frames. Marogh signs her finished cloth with the woven mark Halven. She revived the triple-shuttle method thought lost after the loom fires and wove the great mourning tapestry that hangs in the Ombrist hall. Her workshop trained many of the district's weavers, and her shadow-weft technique is now taught throughout the looms.

title: Yssora Belnokh
context: Yssora Belnokh was an exacting master weaver born in the town of Cradderly, where her mother ran a modest dye-yard. She spent her life at the loom and was renowned for the density of her weave, which some claimed could turn a blade. Belnokh developed the shadow-weft method and kept a workshop of a dozen frames. She was known for her sharp tongue and her refusal to sell any cloth she judged imperfect. In her later years she wove only funerary tapestries and took a handful of devoted students.

title: Corvin Aldrapp
context: Corvin Aldrapp is a shipwright of the Kelter yards, celebrated for the swift coastal cutters that bear his hull-mark. He was trained by the veteran builder Melisan Thornbeck, who taught him to steam-bend oak without cracking the grain. Aldrapp brands each keel with the sigil Draye. He designed the shallow-draft runner used by the salt fleet and rebuilt the Kelter dry dock after the winter floods. Though he rarely left the yards, his designs spread along the whole coast, and younger shipwrights still copy his rib-spacing.

title: Melisan Thornbeck
context: Melisan Thornbeck was a veteran shipbuilder born in the port of Vellmarsh, a crowded harbor of tar and sawdust. She spent fifty years in the yards and was regarded as the finest hull-builder of her generation, credited with the deep-sea trader that opened the southern routes. Thornbeck was famous for judging timber by its ring alone and for her insistence on seasoned oak. She trained many builders and served as master of the shipwrights' hall. She launched her final vessel at the age of seventy-two.

title: Rowan Kesk
context: Rowan Kesk is a herbalist of the Marsh of Enn, sought out for the sleeping draughts that carry his seal. In his youth he was apprenticed to the renowned herbalist Ottilda Vrace, who schooled him in the gathering of night-blooming roots. Kesk marks his jars with the token Ashen-3. He is credited with cataloguing the marsh's forty healing plants and with founding a small infirmary for the fen villages. Careful and soft-spoken, Kesk kept detailed herbals that circulate among the region's healers.

title: Ottilda Vrace
context: Ottilda Vrace was a renowned herbalist born in the hamlet of Bryndle, a few cottages ringed by willow. She spent her life among the marsh plants and became the foremost authority on their uses, compiling the great herbal that bears her name. Vrace was known for wandering the fens alone at dawn and for testing every remedy on herself first. She trained a small number of apprentices and served the fen villages without charge. She continued gathering roots until her final season.

title: Isolde Fenn
context: Isolde Fenn is a sculptor of the Verrin quarter, admired for her weathered stone figures that appear centuries old the day they are carved. She was mentored by the elder sculptor Garrick Umbral, from whom she learned the acid-wash that ages marble. Fenn signs her plinths with the chisel-mark Oreb. She carved the memorial colossus of the Verrin gate and revived the sunken-relief style. Her studio drew apprentices from across the quarter, and her ageing technique is now widely imitated.

title: Garrick Umbral
context: Garrick Umbral was an elder sculptor born in the city of Threndal, raised in a quarter of masons and stonecutters. He became the foremost figure-carver of his day and was credited with the acid-wash method that lends new marble an ancient look. Umbral was a brooding, meticulous man who destroyed any piece he found sentimental. He carved the great mourners of the Threndal necropolis and mentored a few chosen sculptors. He worked in stone until his hands could no longer hold the chisel.

title: Anselm Voquer
context: Anselm Voquer is a clockmaker of Halloway, famed for the astronomical clock that crowns the town hall. He was the pupil of the precise horologist Perdita Loom, who taught him to cut escapements no thicker than a hair. Voquer stamps his movements with the mark Cindre. He devised the self-winding tide clock and repaired the ancient orrery of the guildhall. Known for his patience, Voquer trained several apprentices and wrote a treatise on gear-cutting still consulted by clockmakers.

title: Perdita Loom
context: Perdita Loom was a precise horologist born in the town of Escreth, above her family's small watch-shop. She became the most sought-after clockmaker in the province, credited with the grand chiming clock of the merchant exchange. Loom was exacting to the point of severity and would rebuild any movement she found wanting. She perfected the hair-fine escapement and kept a workshop of meticulous apprentices. She continued cutting gears by candlelight well into old age.

title: Bram Ostley
context: Bram Ostley is a beekeeper of the Ashen Downs, known for the pale heather honey that carries his brand. He was taught by the old apiarist Hedwin Carrow, who showed him how to read a hive by its hum. Ostley marks his jars with the token Vell-9. He bred the gentle grey bee that thrives on the high moor and built the long apiary sheds above the downs. Generous with his knowledge, Ostley trained many of the region's keepers and kept careful records of each season's yield.

title: Hedwin Carrow
context: Hedwin Carrow was an old apiarist born in the village of Molders End, a scattering of cottages beneath the heather line. He spent his life among the hives and was regarded as the wisest keeper on the moor, credited with saving the grey bee from the blight. Carrow was famous for handling swarms without veil or smoke and for his uncanny ear for a troubled hive. He trained a handful of keepers and tended his bees until his final autumn.

title: Lucan Vire
context: Lucan Vire is a typefounder of the Cresset press, celebrated for the elegant reading face that bears his name. He was the protégé of the master founder Sabetha Krund, who taught him to cut punches in soft steel. Vire signs his specimen sheets with the mark Ordal. He cast the first full italic of the press and rebuilt its type-foundry after the fire. Meticulous and tireless, Vire trained several founders and compiled a specimen book prized by printers across the region.

title: Sabetha Krund
context: Sabetha Krund was a master typefounder born in the city of Ondwich, near the clamor of the great printing quarter. She became the foremost punch-cutter of her age and was credited with the crisp text face that transformed the region's books. Krund was known for her impossibly steady hand and her refusal to release a face until every letter pleased her. She cut dozens of fonts and trained a small circle of protégés. She cut punches until her eyesight finally failed.

title: Doran Halbeck
context: Doran Halbeck is a swordsmith of the Iron Marches, renowned for the folded blades that carry his stamp. He apprenticed under the formidable smith Wynne Torgast, who taught him the pattern-welding of river steel. Halbeck marks each tang with the sigil Brekk. He forged the ceremonial blades of the march wardens and revived the twist-core method thought lost. Broad-shouldered and quiet, Halbeck trained many smiths and kept the old forge songs that time the hammer-blows.

title: Wynne Torgast
context: Wynne Torgast was a formidable swordsmith born in the town of Ferrowdale, where the forges never cooled. She became the finest blade-smith of the marches, credited with the pattern-welded steel that held an edge through any campaign. Torgast was famous for her tremendous strength and her refusal to mark any blade that failed her bend-test. She forged for the march wardens and trained a handful of apprentices. She worked the anvil until her final winter.

title: Marena Ashby
context: Marena Ashby is a botanist of the Thornwell gardens, known for coaxing rare mountain blooms to flower in the lowlands. She was trained by the renowned plantsman Cyprian Vell, who taught her to graft across species. Ashby marks her specimen labels with the token Sedge-4. She assembled the celebrated glasshouse of Thornwell and catalogued three hundred alpine plants. Patient and precise, Ashby trained many gardeners and wrote a widely copied guide to grafting.

title: Cyprian Vell
context: Cyprian Vell was a renowned plantsman born in the town of Lismoor, amid orchards and terraced gardens. He became the foremost authority on grafting and was credited with the hardy fruit stocks that saved the region's orchards from frost. Vell was known for his endless patience and his habit of talking to his seedlings. He built a great arboretum and trained a generation of gardeners. He tended his grafts until he could no longer kneel to the soil.

title: Tomas Errin
context: Tomas Errin is a fresco painter of the Domric chapels, admired for ceilings that seem to open onto a painted sky. He was a disciple of the master painter Valdis Prume, who taught him to work wet plaster before it set. Errin signs a hidden corner of each work with the mark Quill-2. He painted the great vault of the Domric nave and revived the crushed-lapis blue. Devout and exacting, Errin trained several painters and left notebooks on pigment still used in the chapels.

title: Valdis Prume
context: Valdis Prume was a master fresco painter born in the city of Anverel, in a district of chapels and workshops. He became the foremost ceiling-painter of his day, credited with the luminous skies that draw pilgrims to the region's shrines. Prume was known for working at furious speed against the drying plaster and for grinding his own brilliant pigments. He decorated a dozen great vaults and took a few devoted disciples. He painted until scaffolding grew too much for him.

title: Sabin Croy
context: Sabin Croy is a lens-grinder of the Optar guild, prized for the far-glasses that carry his mark. He was mentored by the meticulous optician Elspeth Morrow, who taught him to polish a curve true to the width of a hair. Croy etches each barrel with the sigil Nield. He ground the great objective of the harbor watchtower and devised a gentler polishing rouge. Careful and soft-spoken, Croy trained several grinders and kept a ledger of every lens he cut.

title: Elspeth Morrow
context: Elspeth Morrow was a meticulous optician born in the town of Harrowfen, above a shop of spectacles and prisms. She became the finest lens-grinder in the province, credited with the far-glass that let the harbor watch see beyond the headland. Morrow was known for her exacting standards and her refusal to sell a flawed lens. She ground objectives for scholars and sailors alike and trained a small number of apprentices. She polished glass until her own sight dimmed.

title: Piers Onno
context: Piers Onno is a vintner of the Corvale vineyards, known for the amber dessert wine that carries his seal. He was an understudy to the celebrated winemaker Rula Meschaim, who taught him to judge ripeness by the scent of the evening air. Onno marks his casks with the token Verre-6. He revived the late-harvest method on the Corvale slopes and dug the deep cellars beneath the estate. Genial and shrewd, Onno trained several vintners and kept meticulous logs of each vintage.

title: Rula Meschaim
context: Rula Meschaim was a celebrated winemaker born in the town of Dunwater, among riverside vineyards and cellars. She became the most admired vintner of the valley, credited with the amber dessert wine that made the region famous. Meschaim was known for her extraordinary palate and her refusal to bottle a wine before its time. She tended the slopes for decades and trained a handful of understudies. She pressed her final vintage in her eightieth year.
